## **Question 1 \- “Tell me about yourself”**

This question is so important that we’ll dedicate the most time here. I even made an edited video on it:

Here’s the breakdown in written form:

Most people know that your answer to the tell me about you question influences the entire rest of your interview. But what most people miss is that a bad answer gets you rejected.

You never get a second chance to make a first impression. Most hiring managers make up their mind in the first 3 minutes. When hiring over 50 PMs myself, I didn’t always choose to reject someone over this question, but I did reject many.

So let’s dive right into the three main things you need to know:

1. How to structure a strong answer using the addressing weaknesses framework  
2. Making the role you are interviewing for seem like a great next step in your narrative  
3. How to avoid the most common mistakes people make

### **1\. How to structure a strong answer using the addressing weaknesses framework**

This is the most powerful way to answer this question. The trick is to ask: What are the weaknesses in my candidacy?

Interviewers are looking at your resume while you’re answering this question, or just looked at it. They have formed certain opinions about weaknesses in your candidacy. You need to address what they perceive are weaknesses and shine a spotlight on your strengths.

The fastest and most objective way to do this is to return to the job description. Yes, most of those things are copy pasted junk. But they still are the best source of signal for you on the job.

Let’s say I’m this PM from Microsoft:

* 3 years at Microsoft, 1 year at Wayfair  
* MBA, Deloitte before that

And I’m applying for this job at Tinder:

* Working on AI, ML including on the Vision Pro  
* Looking for 6 years of consumer growth experience

The job is looking for 6+ years of consumer growth experience. But the candidate was a consultant before her MBA, so the specific consumer growth experience is about 4.5 years. So this is the first weakness.

The job is also focused on new hardware platforms like the Apple Vision Pro, but the PM doesn’t have experience with that. So this is the second weakness.

Finally, the job is at Tinder, in the dating realm. The interviewer is naturally going to resonate more with dating candidates. The candidate hasn’t been in dating.

The answer we come up with should address all three of these weaknesses head on. And it should emphasize the candidate’s strengths:

Since graduating from my MBA at Duke in 2019, I’ve been a PM at Wayfair and Microsoft.

At Microsoft I launched Copilot for Teams, for which I got the opportunity to present on stage.

I also worked on Teams across a variety of hardware devices, including MacOS, Windows, Chromepad, Android, and iOS.

Although I’ve been a PM in consumer products for 4.5 years, before my MBA, at Deloitte I actually worked as a PM consultant for a variety of other consumer products. So my total time as a PM is about 7 years.

One of my clients at Deloitte was actually a competitor of Tinder’s, a large public company.

This is how you actually influence the course of the rest of the interview, You have head on brought up the topics that the interviewer might consider weak about your candidacy.

The big mistake that most candidates make is that they let these weaknesses linger in the interviewer’s mind. So the follow-up questions from the interviewer all revolve around those weaknesses. On the other hand, this framing lets you lead with strengths.

### **2\. Making the role you are interviewing for seem like a great next step in your narrative**

Have you ever asked someone if they wanted something and they just felt disinterested? This is exactly how you do NOT want your interviewer to feel

People who get the job seem excited about the role they are interviewing for. Let’s go back to our example. This role at Tinder is about things like working on Vision Pro and AI. You should incorporate your interest in those.

Here’s how you could add this in to your answer:

With my experience working on Teams Copilot using GPT-4 at Microsoft, I’m very excited about this role.

I believe that AI will be at the forefront of all next gen products.

So although things are going well at Microsoft, I was really excited when I saw this job posting and had to apply.

The key to answering these questions is realizing that humans think about careers linearly. Even though your career has likely been a rocky path, help the interviewer understand the straight lines that bring you here.

For our candidate, she has connected that back with AI. Make your own linkages

### **3\. Addressing the key mistakes that most people make**

#### **Mistake 1: Bringing up things that they can’t dig into**

All the details you bring up, you should be able to tell lots of details about if they ask follow-up questions. Refresh the details before your interview.

You should just have a highlight in your answer. But be ready to go deeper.

#### **Mistake 2: Going way too long**

This is by far the most common reason I have rejected candidates. They just take up most of the interview time. Practice this question before the interview and have a hard stop of 2 minutes.

Do not go longer than 2 minutes.

#### **Mistake 3: Not having an easy to follow narrative**

This looks something like a jumble of a structure. Jumping from one job to the next.

Whether it’s chronological, or reverse chronological, try to have some flow to your answer. The best way to do this is to draft your answer to this question before every interview. Then record yourself on video and finesse your response

### **Putting It All Together: Example Answer**

Now let’s put that all together for our good answer.

But this time \- let’s have a new example. Let’s pretend I’m a college student ([more info](https://www.news.aakashg.com/p/how-to-become-a-pm-with-no-experience#%C2%A7your-tell-me-about-yourself-should-address-all-concerns)), and I’m interested in an APM program at Spotify. My weaknesses are I don’t have a PM internship, I haven’t worked in the music industry, and I went to a middling school.

I am really excited about this role at Spotify. I have been using Spotify for over 10 years now. I constantly have ideas for how it could be better.

That’s because I actually worked on several side projects in college in a similar space. One of my favorites was Generate a Song with AI. This was a website I released that leveraged the latest APIs from Meta.

With my CS background, I was able to build the app myself. And I grew it to 5,000 users. The fun I had with that makes me really excited about Spotify’s APM program.

I want to spend my career in product management. When I did my software engineering internship at Amazon, I loved working with PMs. It made me realize that is the job I want to take up in my career.

It’s the intersection of my technical, music, and builder talents.

How did this answer stack up against our three criteria?

1. The answer addresses all three weaknesses.  
2. The answer also expresses interest in the role.  
3. The answer also is quite concise and includes details about stories of coding side projects that the candidate is ready to go deeper on.

*Now we’re going to give the same treatment to the other 11 most common questions.*

## **Question 2 \- “What is your current pay?”**

This question is not legal [everywhere](https://chat.openai.com/share/d06dd44d-765d-4268-bb0e-8b826fce844c) (\~1/2 US states, EU). But it is legal some places (UK, Australia, India)\! Several people have pinged me in the last week after being asked it.

There’s a couple keys to keep in mind when answering this question:

1. You want to avoid sharing your current pay  
2. You want to have numbers ready to share  
3. Your numbers should be factual

Let’s get into each.

### **1\. You want to avoid sharing your current pay**

As much as possible, you want to avoid or get around this question. The reason is: it can really only hurt you.

Your pay is going to become their anchor. They’ll come in around it. The best case is they come in a bit above. The worst case is they come in way below.

Contrary to what you think: they’re not going to disqualify you for it. And if they do, it’s probably not a great place to work for.

So the best thing to do is avoidance.

You do this in two steps:

1. Not answering  
2. Flipping a question back to them

It sounds like this:

**Interviewer**: What’s your current pay?

**Interviewee**: I’m doing well. I’m really interested in the entire package \- compensation, culture, scope. What is the range for this role?

### **2\. You want to have numbers ready to share**

The way to avoid is with numbers. You want to share numbers that they can anchor instead. So you want to have something up your pocket.

So when the follow-up, you give them those numbers:

**Interviewer**: I was actually curious what your current entire package is?

**Interviewee**: I’d prefer not to share. I can share the range I expect for this role.

### **3\. Your numbers should be factual**

With respect to those numbers, the factuality of your numbers, that’s where there’s a range of potential responses. The more convincing the better.

So let’s say you’re applying to a big company that’s on Layoffs.fyi, then that’s good data. Or if you’re applying to a VC backed startup, Carta’s data for companies at that round is good data.

You should say something like this:

**Interviewee**: Based on Carta’s range for Series C SaaS companies, I expect cash of $180-$240K and equity equivalent to 0.015-0.02% per year.

**Interviewer**: Okay.

Otherwise, if you’re relying on Glassdoor or guesses, then it’s tougher. You’ll say something like this:

**Interviewee**: The range for PMs in this areas is about $80-$100K. I’ve had a few friends who recently received that compensation with similar experience and similar sized companies. One was at Burnam & Stone. The other was at Thevy.

**Interviewer**: But I don’t think those comps apply to us. What is your current range?

**Interviewee**: I think my market value is that much and I have spoken with other companies in that range.

**Interviewer**: Okay.

It’s tougher to jostle with the interviewer, but if you can get away with not sharing, you tend to be better off.

So, to summarize:

* Lean towards not sharing  
* If pressed, share a number  
* Then defend that number after being pressed

---

## **Question 3 \- “What are your compensation expectations?”**

Depending on where you live, this question also may not be legal. But people are asked it regularly.

The basic structure you want to respond with is:

* The high end of the band for this level  
* I am concerned about the whole package  
* I am keen to see how the interviews proceed in terms of fit

The answer is different than the above question, because, **you don't want to throw out a number**. You want to flip it back at them in this interview or before so you know their range.

**Interviewer:** What are your compensation expectations?

**Interviewee:** I was actually wondering what your range for this role is?

Once you know their range, (helpful in places like the EU and Colorado where they have to share), you say something like:

**Interviewer:** What are your compensation expectations?

**Interviewee:** The recruiter shared a $245-$275K band. I would like the high end of the band. At the same time, I’m also evaluating the whole package. I’m keen to understand benefits, equity, and scope. I’m also looking forward to seeing my cultural fit with the other interviewers.

That’s why it’s very valuable to ask for their range in the first interview with a recruiter.

---

## **Question 4 \- “Why do you want to work here?”**

There’s a few key principles when answering this questions:

1. It’s all about authenticity  
2. Structure your answer  
3. Bring in facts

### **1\. It’s all about authenticity**

This question is all about authenticity. You need to shine full of honest energy about what intrigues about the role and the company.

This isn’t the time for “umms” and “hms.” Or a “by the books” answer.

It’s the time to jump out of your Zoom Box with excitement. It’s time to show them via body language how excited you are.

### **2\. Structure your answer**

While it’s not the time for a “by the books” answer, a structure that works well is:

* I love the mission & vision  
* The role is a great fit for my career goals & experience  
* I've enjoyed meeting the people & the company's values

Then you add in the actual information about the company, role, and people you've met. It sounds something like this:

**Interviewer**: So. Why do you want to work at Pendo?

**Interviewee**:

* I’m a huge fan of Pendo’s mission to the be the best all-in-one software for PMs. as a PM myself, I feel like this product is just needed in the world. At my last company, event analytics were a mess.  
* This specific role also draws me to our conversation today. I’m hugely interested in building out the UX for your analytics product to accommodate all of a PM’s needs.  
* I’ve enjoyed meeting everyone at Pendo. Everyone smiled while walking by in the hall. Pendozers clearly live the value of loving their work. This type of venture backed startup environment is what I thrive most in.

That type of an answer hits all the main points.

### **3\. Bring in facts**

What really makes these answers stand out are the little facts:

* At my last company, event analytics were a mess.  
* Everyone smiled while walkign by in the hall.

The more specific, contextual anecdotes you can sprinkle in, the better.

## **Question 5 \- “Why this job?”**

You’d be surprised how many candidates don’t seize this question.

Remember these three things:

1. Bring out the enthusiasm  
2. Speak to concerns about your level  
3. Speak to concerns about industry and functional expertise

### **1\. Bring out the enthusiasm**

This is another question where they need to see the light in your eye.

What I recommend doing is literally shifting forward in your chair.

It’s time to bring out the charm here. You want them to think that you’ve dreamed about this job.

Of course, you have to be realistic. Which bring us to two and three…

### **2\. Speak to concerns about your level**

There’s always going to be some concerns about your level. Maybe they think you’re too junior. Or too senior.

You want this question to address them. It might even sound like this if there’s an obvious discrepancy:

Although I’ve been a manager in my last role, I’ve actually gone back and forth from manager and IC recently. And for this area, consumer search, I would really like to be an IC.

I think that Search is a really exciting place to dig into the data, execute on PRDs and features, really QA.

I like the idea of doing more of that in my next step.

### **3\. Speak to concerns about industry and functional expertise**

There’s always going to be some concerns about your industry or your functional background. They might think you’ve been in different industries, or haven’t done that type of PM.

Add detail around why that weakness isn’t so in this question.

Let’s say they’re worried whether you have platform PM experience:

I’m really excited about the platform aspect of this job.

I actually pinch hit for a colleague two years back on a platform role. She went on mat leave. So I picked up her area and charter.

It was very interesting to be one step removed from features. I enjoyed it.

I really enjoying supporting my PM counterparts.

Including details where you are weak, and putting it into an overall structure, is the key with this question.

---

## **Question 6 \- “Why are you leaving your current job?”**

It's key to focus on the future and what you're looking for, rather than dwelling on any negatives of your current role.

Saying bad things about your current role is a bad look. Here's the types of things you should talk about instead:

* Emphasize Growth and New Challenges  
* Align with the Company’s Direction  
* Mention Team Dynamics and Culture Fit

It sounds like this:

I’m seeking a new role to further my growth and take on fresh challenges. In my current position, I’ve had great opportunities to work on \[specific projects or achievements\], which has been incredibly rewarding.

However, I’m now looking to step into a role with broader responsibilities, especially in areas like \[the role\].

What attracts me to \[Company\] is your innovative work in \[specific fields or technologies\] and the collaborative culture you’ve built.

I’m excited about the potential to contribute to your team and help drive \[Company\]’s goals forward.

---

## **Question 7 \- “What is your greatest weakness?”**

This question is easy to mess up. Remember to:

1. Be honest  
2. Structure a good answer  
3. Showcase your growth mindset

### **1\. Be honest**

This is not the time for a fake weakness\! Even people who are honest tend to choose **a** weakness instead of their greatest one.

This is a mistake.

Just be honest. What performance feedback do you always get? It’s probably something innate, related to your personality. (But don’t tell your interviewer that…)

### **2\. Structure a good answer**

That means it’s something you’re probably working on.

That’s what the structure of your answer should show:

* I'm always improving  
* My most recent performance cycle had this feedback  
* Here's how I'm working on it

### **3\. Showcase your growth mindset**

The key for this question is to show you don't have a fixed mindset.

Of course, still be respectful of the question and talk about a weakness. But end your response with how you're growing.

It sounds like this:

My biggest weakness is that I can let my stress show.

This is something I’ve gotten as performance feedback in the form of motivating my team, or dealing with tough times.

But I’m always improving.

In fact, I’ve made a lot of progress recently.

In my last performance cycle, my manager called out that many peers had put that I did a great job pulling the team up.

I’ve been working on this weakness by catching myself in tough times.

Those are the easiest to get away from me.

So I like to physically get up and go for a walk.

It’s been working well. I hope to keep improving with more experience and wisdom and years under my belt.

---

## **Question 8 \- “What is your biggest failure?”**

Like the last question, you want to be honest with this question and choose a great failure. But it’s not as important to actually choose your life’s greatest personal failure.

For this question:

1. Choose your greatest work failure  
2. Make it seem like a failure that’s reasonable to fall into  
3. Show how you’ve grown

### **1\. Choose your greatest work failure**

Personal things generally aren’t a good fit here. I know this is controversial advice. But I’d focus on a PM work failure.

Every PM can relate to PM work failures. And most PMs can understand a work failure as your greatest failure.

So it allows for better empathy and helps you advanced the interview forward in the direction you want. This should be a golden rule of interviews: always advance your agenda when answering their questions.

### **2\. Make it seem like a failure that’s reasonable to fall into**

You want to help dig your grave for them. Help them empathize.

Freely admit your mistakes, but help them understand the context of why you made those mistakes.

You don’t want the failure to sound like a personal flaw.

Bad:

I missed responding to the thread for two weeks, so it cause problems down the line…

Good:

There were competing requests from stakeholders.

The execs wanted one thing, sales another, and customers yet another.

I ended up going the way of execs.

But it was a mistake to be a yes man.

### **3\. Show how you’ve grown**

The structure for your response should be:

* I can choose a work failure  
* Here's what I did wrong  
* Here's how I grew

They may drill down on why it's your biggest failure or what you did wrong. So choose a real example. But end on a high note \- show you have a growth mindset.

---

## **Question 9 \- “Fast forward three years. What will you be then?”**

There’s no right answer to this question. It’s still important to be you. Here’s what to remember:

1. Showcase introspection  
2. Show interest in career growth  
3. Incorporate the company and role

### **1\. Showcase introspection**

They want you to be introspective in this question. You should mention dimensions of PM that you want to get better at.

### **2\. Show interest in career growth**

It’s about showing that you have a growth mindset and what to get better at the PM craft.

A lot of people will just mention the title, how many people they manage, what their scope is.

These things matter. But an A+ answer is introspective and growth-focused.

### **3\. Incorporate the company and role**

Finally, be sure to make the company and specific role part of your narrative\!

You should always be selling this role as perfect for you.

It sounds something like this:

In five years, I see myself leading major projects here at \[Company\]. I've already driven a 40% increase in user retention and broke into new markets in my last role.

One area I want to get better at is customer discovery. I see myself actually driving the discovery for those projects.

What excites me about \[Company\] is your work in \[specific area or technology\].

I believe my background fits well with your goals, and there’s a lot we can achieve together.

I’m also keen on learning from the team here, especially about \[specific company strengths or technologies\]."

---

## **Question 10 \- “What’s something everyone takes for granted that you think is hogwash?**

This question is one where they are trying to break you out of your interview preparation. So it’s not exactly about a structured answer.

It’s about:

1. Showcasing the unique you  
2. Showcasing a strong ability to think  
3. Using it as an opportunity to emphasize what you want

### **1\. Showcasing the unique you**

You have somethings that just get you passionate. They are your countervailing opinions. Take a few minutes to brainstorm them.

You can literally choose any topic. It doesn’t need to be product management. It can be your favorite hobby.

The key is to show that you can be an independent thinker for this question. Not that you can repeat back an answer from this article.

### **2\. Showcasing a strong ability to think**

Once you identify your topic, you should make it crystal clear to your interviewer what the thing is.

What you choose must:

* **Actually be something everyone takes for granted**: it can’t be something smart people actually know isn’t true  
* **That you have some persuasive insight why it’s wrong**: it can’t just be your feeling, you have to have a story, data point, or anecdote to back it up

If you show strong thinking, you will be well ahead of most.

### **3\. Using it as an opportunity to emphasize what you want**

The 4-D chess way to answer this question is to emphasize something you want to showcase. Let’s return all the way to Question 1 and our Microsoft PM applying to Tinder.

One of the areas that the PM didn’t have experience was platforms like the Apple Vision Pro. Some of the other candidates would surely have experience with visual design for AR. (They might work at Niantic, for instance.)

So the PM could use this time to give a next level response there. It could be something like this:

The belief everyone takes for granted I would like to call out is:

The illusion of hyper-realism as a panacea

Everyone seems to think that the way to AR graphics success is to be more realistic. But I don’t think that’s everything.

Actually when I use tools like the Meta Quest to check how Teams functions, I’ve noticed that it’s better to have a distinctive visual design.

I think this is proven out by how the Vision Pro was demo’ed at WWDC. I was so wow’ed by them I actually tweeted about it.

It’s all a raised bevel design.

So that’s what I believe is hogwash: that hyper-realism is everything in AR graphics.

This helps establish the candidate as actually strong in the space of Vision Pro design.

---

## **Question 11 \- “What work accomplishment are you most proud of?”**

The interviewer is hoping to gain insight into what gives you pride and the significance of your accomplishments.

So here’s what to remember:

1. Choose a story that has an arc  
2. Make sure it’s something with big impact  
3. Try to leverage something at the intersection of what you’re great at and what they want

### **1\. Choose a story that has an arc**

The best story arc to use for this question is the U:

![The Six Shapes of All Stories - with Entrepreneurial Tales - Craft Your  Content][image3]

[Image](https://www.craftyourcontent.com/six-story-structures-entrepreneurship/)

If you can display that it was a challenging situation, that makes it memorable. And you want to bring them along for the ride so they fell your pain.

Then you climb out of the hole with them towards triumph. This helps them follow along the thread and remember your victory come time for the hiring committee to sit down and all discuss together.

This question often tends to be a “personal favorite.” It’s one people remember. So choose one of your best stories.

### **2\. Make sure it’s something with big impact**

You want to have some numbers in your results. And then give context to them:

Bad:

We increased revenue $14M

Good:

We increased revenue 11% with a single feature, it was $14M annually. It was great to smash our OKRs for the year in a quarter

### **3\. Try to leverage something at the intersection of what you’re great at and what they want**

The final note is to find something at the intersection of what you’re good at and what they want.

This is one of the storytelling questions. It’s a shame to waste it on a skill that isn’t relevant to the job.

Especially pay attention to the level. Is it an IC or a managerial role? Choose that type of story. Is it managing a team of 1 or 10? Choose that **level** of story.

### **Putting It All Together: Example Answer**

Let’s say you’re interviewing for a role as a PM on the news feed at LinkedIn:

A work accomplishment I’m most proud of was in 2018 on the news feed team at Meta.

If you remember, in 2018, trust in Meta was at an all-time low. After Cambridge Analytica in 2016, things kept going down.

This was a problem for my team, since we were focused on Facebook Trust.

So one of the challenging things for us was to weight trust with initiatives by the growth team. Sometimes, we would be undoing each other’s features.

So I worked on a growth initiative hand in hand with the growth team that was a big win for the both of us.

I hypothesized that we could increase the content of news organization videos in your feed that you don’t follow that helped growth and trust.

I worked with the team to incept the hypothesis and took it all the way to our Sr Director’s.

Everyone had their eyes on the test the next week.

I shared results regularly and brought everyone along. It was our biggest win of the quarter. We ended up helping the growth team hit their OKRs by 3x.

This helps them really understand you can help the overall news feed product org in a collaborative manner.

## **Question 12 \- “Describe a scenario in which you had to say no to an idea or project”**

This is an [infamous PM skill](https://www.news.aakashg.com/p/how-to-say-no-as-a-pm-advanced-tips). You have to be able to say no.

There’s a couple things, therefore, that you should do with this story:

1. Make it clear you say no often and have chosen a high impact example  
2. Choosing a story that adds to your symphony of skills  
3. Getting into how you said not and why it wasn’t easy

### **1\. Make it clear you say no often and have chosen a high impact example**

PMs are always saying no. And you should be too. So your answer should make this clear.

You shouldn’t just choose the last time you said no.

Think back to an example that was actually a tough no, where you remember the texture of why.

### **2\. Choosing a story that adds to your symphony of skills**

Also think back to the addressing weaknesses framework. That should always be your north star. How can you do that here?

This question often comes towards the end of a behavioral interview.

So look back at your other answers. Choose a story that will emphasize the weakness you have least convincingly beaten back.

### **3\. Getting into how you said not and why it wasn’t easy**

And make sure the story was a tough no\! I can’t emphasize this enough.

It can’t have been en easy no. Show all the depth of how hard the no was, and then all the work you did to justify it.

Use it as an opportunity to highlight your great customer [discovery](https://www.news.aakashg.com/p/advanced-techniques-continuous-discovery).

---

## **4\. Timeless principles**

There’s a couple timeless principles I also want to mention that didn’t make it into the specific questions:

* Ask for time  
* Structure your response  
* Use the rule of three to structure  
* Explain the structure of what you're going to say  
* Then go through each point and say it  
* Then repeat back your outline  
* End with a bang  
* Be concise

---

## **How to prepare**

When it comes to preparing, the key is list out 4-5 stories from each of your past roles (or whatever results in 10-15 stories total) and practice out the details for these.

You’d be surprised how many things your forget about the details. Try to go back and lack at the feature. Remember the metrics. Ping a former colleague to verify your details about it.

Once you have these rich 10-15 stories, you can apply them to many of the behavioral questions we went over.

---

## **Most common mistakes**

I see candidates making the same common mistakes. Don’t be one of those:

1. **Going too long**: I just can’t emphasize it enough. No longer than 2 minutes at a time.  
2. **Not addressing every weakness with every interviewer**: Emphasize a diversity of skills and hit all your weaknesses. Otherwise you’ll be hit with a rejection on that weakness you didn’t address.  
3. **Losing structure**: PMs have to communicate well. In an interview, the way is structure. Don’t just speak flow of consciousness.

---

## **For questions that surprise you?**

Finally, here’s your playbook if they hit you with a question that surprises you:

* Ask for time  
* Structure a response  
* Redirect to topics you are comfortable with

Never just jump into a response when you don't have a good one. Always feel free to redirect to a strong story or point you want to convey.

---

## **Final Words**

There’s so many behavioral questions out there, and there’s no right answer to any of them. The key is to assess what your interviewer wants and what you can truthfully say.

Instead of spending too much time on the context, also spend time on being mentally prepared and practiced. Get your sleep. Be confident. Power pose.

*Do what you need to execute in interview.*

## ***1\. The First Principles***

*Let’s begin by building your first principles understanding of how to execute in response to this question:*

### ***Principle 1: Flip Weaknesses Into Strengths***

***The trick is to ask**: what are the main weaknesses that someone would have looking at my [resume](https://www.news.aakashg.com/p/ultimate-guide-the-pm-resume-examples) and [LinkedIn](https://www.news.aakashg.com/p/how-to-optimize-your-linkedin-profile)?*

*You want to identify the 1-3 most important weaknesses. Then, you need to devise how you are going to **flip them into strengths**.*

*You’re not going to answer untruthfully, but you are going to answer in a sales pitch.*

### ***Principle 2: Show a Through-line to this Job Now***

*Speaking of sales, you are not trying to answer a cross-examination of your past. You don’t need to highlight everything. You want to sell the most relevant experiences, and spend the majority of your time, where you want them to focus.*

*They’re going to ask you questions about what you say, so keep it focused on the things that show you’re qualified for that job \- and there’s a natural through-line in your background to getting there.*

*In a way, you’re subtly answering “why this role and company” by the details you choose.*

### ***Principle 3: 2 Minutes is the sweet spot***

*The most common mistake that people make it so to get caught up in telling their own chronological story.*

*And they drone on and on endlessly while the interviewer checks out. I can’t emphasize it enough. This happened to me regularly as an interviewer at Apollo and Affirm.*

*Go for right around 2 minutes.*

### ***You Must Practice, Practice, Practice***

*Above all, a key for success for this question is to actually record yourself giving the response the night or two before the interview.*

*You want to hit the first question of your interviews like a choreographed dance, not off the cuff.*

*And analyzing and improving yourself is the key.*

*Let’s get into exactly that \- improving the responses of 3 real-world candidates:*

---

## ***2\. Case Study: Aspiring PM***

*Alright, let’s work on creating a great response for an aspiring PM. Here was our one-hour session:*

*We managed to go from a 4/10 to a 9/10. These are the key takeaways you should remember from each round.*

#### ***Round 1: 4/10***

*The crucial lesson here is that **you need to get identify the right weakness**:*

* *Manish thought his confidence and use of filler words gave him a 4/10. I disagreed. For me, **it was because he didn’t properly address his biggest weakness**.*  
* *That was because **I disagreed about what his biggest weakness was**. He thought it was technical depth. But really, it was his PM experience and consulting internship.*  
* *Together, **we found stories from his past that helped highlight his PM-specific experience**. We also talked about how important it is for students to do projects, groups, and other activities to plug their gaps.*

#### ***Round 2: 6/10***

*The key lesson here is **the importance of structure and relevance**:*

* *Manish improved by categorizing his career into three clear phases, making his story easier to follow. He focused more on PM-relevant experiences, especially his work at the tech company.*  
* *However, **his response was still too long at over 3 minutes**. This highlights the challenge of balancing detail with conciseness.*  
* *We learned that **it's crucial to practice timing** your response to hit the 2-minute sweet spot.*

#### ***Round 3: 7/10***

*This round emphasized **the power of specific examples and quantifiable impact**:*

* *Manish included more detailed stories, like reducing onboarding time from 72 to 24 hours. He quantified his impact: acquiring 30,000 customers in six months.*  
* ***He started showing genuine passion for PM**, mentioning steps he's taken to learn more about the field.*  
* *However, in adding these details, **his response grew even longer**. This underscores the need to ruthlessly prioritize what to include.*

#### ***Round 4: 8/10***

*The focus here was on **tailoring the response to the specific company and role**:*

* *Manish demonstrated research into Travelport's API, showing genuine interest. He connected his past experiences directly to the requirements of the role.*  
* *His energy and confidence significantly improved, projecting enthusiasm. While shorter than before, **his response was still over the ideal length at 2:30**.*  
* *This round highlighted that **company research and enthusiasm can significantly boost your pitch**.*

#### ***Final Round: 9/10***

*The final round showcased **the importance of addressing weaknesses and ending strong**:*

* *Manish finally hit the 2-minute target while maintaining substance. He proactively addressed potential concerns about his background. He emphasized his commitment to PM through self-study efforts.*  
* ***He ended with a strong, confident pitch** for why he's ideal for the role.*  
* *This round proved that **with practice, you can craft a response that's concise, relevant, and compelling**.*

*The progression from 4/10 to 9/10 demonstrates how targeted practice and feedback can dramatically improve your "Tell Me About Yourself" response. It's not just about reciting your history, but strategically presenting your story to address the interviewer's key concerns and highlight your strengths.*

---

## ***3\. Case Study: Mid-Career PM***

*Now, let’s move to a mid-career PM. We’ll help Kartik go from a 4.5 to a 9/10:*

#### ***Round 1: 4.5/10***

*The crucial lesson here was similar to Manish’s session \- that **you need to identify and address your biggest weaknesses**:*

* *Kartik thought his weakness was limited mobile app experience. I disagreed. For me, **it was his job-hopping history and recent career break** that were the biggest red flags.*  
* *We also identified that **he was underselling his most relevant experience** at iimjobs.com.*  
* *Together, **we strategized how to reframe these potential weaknesses as strengths**.*

#### ***Round 2: 6.5/10***

*The key takeaway is **the power of leading with your strongest, most relevant experience**:*

* *Kartik led with his iimjobs.com experience, which was directly relevant to the B2C mobile app role. He included a specific project (short-form content feature) with quantifiable results (20% adoption).*  
* ***We addressed the career break by reframing it** as productive time working with Product Growth.*  
* *However, we still needed to tackle the job-hopping concern and tighten the overall response.*

#### ***Round 3: 8/10***

*This round emphasized **the importance of structure and highlighting growth**:*

* *Kartik organized his response into three clear sections: recent, B2C, and earlier experiences. He emphasized how each role contributed to his growth as a PM.*  
* ***We saw how a well-structured response can make varied experience look purposeful**.*  
* *The main missing piece was a strong connection to QuitSure's specific role and mission.*

#### ***Round 4: 7/10***

*This round showed that **even good content can fall flat with poor framing**:*

* *Kartik attempted to address job-hopping upfront, but the framing was too negative. We learned that **it's crucial to maintain a positive tone throughout the response**.*  
* *The ending improved by showing interest in a stable opportunity, but still lacked personal connection.*  
* *This demonstrated the challenge of balancing addressing weaknesses with selling strengths.*

#### ***Final Round: 9/10***

*The final round showcased **how to craft a compelling narrative that addresses concerns while highlighting strengths**:*

* *Kartik reframed his varied experience as preparation for a dynamic startup role. He maintained focus on his most relevant experience while briefly touching on earlier roles.*  
* ***We added a personal connection to QuitSure's mission**, mentioning his father's struggle to quit smoking.*  
* *This round hit all the key points: addressing weaknesses, showcasing strengths, and connecting to the role.*

*The progression from 4.5/10 to 9/10 demonstrates how targeted practice and feedback can dramatically improve your "Tell Me About Yourself" response, especially for mid-career PMs with complex backgrounds.*

---

## ***4\. Case Study: Experienced PM & Coach***

*Finally, let’s help Kent McDonald, an experienced product manager and coach, improve his "Tell Me About Yourself" response from a 6/10 to a 9/10.*

*Here are the key takeaways from each round:*

#### ***Round 1: 5/10***

*The crucial lesson here is that **even seasoned professionals can miss the mark on addressing key concerns**:*

* *Kent thought his response was decent, giving himself a 6/10. I disagreed, rating it a 5/10. For me, **the main issue was that he didn't address the elephant in the room** \- his recent lack of insurance industry experience.*  
* *We identified that **his biggest perceived weakness wasn't what he thought**. He was concerned about strategic leadership experience, but the real issue was his recent work outside of insurance.*  
* *Together, **we strategized how to highlight his insurance background**, including his time at Nationwide and Blue Cross Blue Shield, even if it wasn't his most recent experience.*

#### ***Round 2: 7/10***

*The key takeaway is **the power of addressing perceived weaknesses head-on**:*

* *Kent restructured his response to lead with his insurance experience, tackling the main concern. He highlighted his work with data platforms, aligning with the job requirements.*  
* *However, **we realized we needed to do more to sell Kent for this specific role at Duck Creek**. Interviewers might find this new story actually created a new weakness.*  
* *The response could use specific metrics and a compelling reason for wanting this particular position.*

#### ***Round 3: 8/10***

*This round emphasized **the importance of adding specifics and tying experiences directly to the role**:*

* *Kent included more details about his work, like improving claims processing efficiency at Blue Cross Blue Shield.*  
* *He connected his varied experience to Duck Creek's needs, showing how he could apply his knowledge.*  
* ***We identified that enthusiasm and company-specific knowledge were still missing**, which could take the response from good to great.*

#### ***Final Round: 9/10***

*The final iteration showcased **how to blend experience, enthusiasm, and company knowledge**:*

* *Kent started with genuine excitement about the opportunity, setting a positive tone. He directly addressed how his background in insurance and data platforms aligned with Duck Creek's needs.*  
* ***Kent incorporated specific elements from the job description**, mentioning his Agile experience and MBA. He tied his experience to Duck Creek's growth goals, demonstrating he'd researched the company.*  
* *The energy level increased significantly, projecting authentic interest in the role.*

*Kent's journey from a 6/10 to a 9/10 shows that **even experienced professionals can significantly improve their pitch with targeted feedback and practice**.*

## ***5\. Framework to Improve Yourself***

*So, now it’s your turn to evaluate your own response. As you can deduce:*

* *The most important thing is to get the right weakness*  
* *Then you need to get feedback on whether you’ve answered it*  
* *And make sure that you’re under time, with confidence and poise*

### ***The most important thing is to get the right weakness***

*Clearly, the key from our example interviews, with each interviewer, we had a disagreement about what is the most important weakness.*

*So let’s talk about how to think about weaknesses. Generally, there are four major weaknesses to worry about \- from most to least common:*

1. *Years of experience*  
2. *Career breaks, job hopping, [layoffs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=afPDnG-gcgY)*  
3. *Size and complexity of teams managed*  
4. *The industries you’ve worked in and how recently*  
5. *Your experience in the specific product areas of the role*

#### ***1\. Years of Experience***

*If a job description is asking for 8 years of B2B SaaS experience and you only have 5 years of it, you want to address it.*

*You might bring up related experience why it’s similar, or extra work you’ve done on the side… the solution is up to you.*

*But if you don’t meet years of experience, it’s always the most important weakness.*

#### ***2\. Career breaks, job hopping, layoffs***

*The next most important weakness might be controversial to some, but I believe it strongly. People discriminate against folks with breaks, job hopping, or layoffs.*

*This is what we covered with both Manish and Kartik above. So even if you have the domain and functional expertise in terms of breadth, they might not think you have the depth.*

*You have to be careful to paint depth and high performance in your prior career.*

#### ***3\. Size and complexity of teams managed***

*As a PM of any type, they are going to care about how many engineers and designers, user researchers and product analysts that you helmed the primary PM role for.*

*On top of that, if you’re a manager, they’re going to be interested in how many people directly managed.*

*It’s possible to be below the requirements, but you have to have a clear story for why. Did you have an interim role of a bigger size, for instance? Use the response to answer.*

#### ***4\. The industries you’ve worked in and how recently***

*These days, companies are waiting for PMs with experience close to their industry. This is especially true for the B2B/B2C divide. Companies want experience on their side of the aisle.*

*Usually, companies will construct a specific background they want. For instance, Apollo was looking for a PM with growth B2C gaming \+ B2B experience. As a result, they hired me.*

*You want to figure out what the company wants and sell that. You may need to widen the lens \- instead of sales tech, B2B SaaS, for instance. But you must address industry experience.*

#### ***5\. Your experience in the specific product areas of the role***

*The final of the 5 important weaknesses is your experience in a specific product area: eg, growth, core, platform, [AI](https://www.news.aakashg.com/p/how-to-become-an-ai-pm) PM.*

*On top of that, companies often want experience in a specific area. For instance, when hiring for activation at Apollo, I wanted someone who had done onboarding in sales tech.*

*So you want to get as close to the specifics of the role you’d be in and make it a clear strength, especially if it’s not clear from your resume.*

*That covers it for the 5 most important weaknesses to prioritize flipping.*

#### ***Notice what’s not a most important weakness***

*In coaching sessions, everyone thought their weakness was a skill like: technical, or strategic leadership.*

*More often than not, these tend not to be the most important weakness.*

*Usually, it has to do with specific facts about your background instead of skills you have as a PM. The main exception is if they need a specifically technical PM in an area of developer tools or APIs.*

### ***Then you need to get feedback on whether you’ve answered it***

*The next thing to do is see how you’ve answered the weakness. Have you cited specific examples?*

*Do they have metrics? Is your role towards the metrics clear?*

*You want to bring it all together.*

*I highly recommend practicing with interview partners for this. Alternatively, use an automatic transcription tool like Riverside, YouTube, or Otter to get a transcript of your video.*

*Then plug that into ChatGPT, or your favorite LLM, with the prompt:*

*\#\# Instructions:*

*Act as an interview coach. You are proficient at giving feedback on transcripts of responses to help interviewees secure job offers. I'm going to share a draft response I gave on video \- translated via transcript \- for the "Tell me about yourself" question.*

*\#\# Relevant Information:*

*\- Company: \[Company Name\]*

*\- Position: \[Job Title\]*

*\- Current Role: \[Your current position\]*

*\- Years of Experience: \[Number of years\]*

*\- Key Skills: \[List 2-3 key skills\]*

*\- Perceived Weakness: \[State your biggest weakness\]*

*\#\# Feedback Request:*

*Please provide feedback on how well I:*

*\- Remained concise and engaging*

*\- Demonstrated fit for the specific role*

*\- Addressed my weakness and turned it into a strength*

*\- Highlighted relevant experiences and skills*

*\- Told a compelling personal/professional story*

*\#\# Transcript:*

*\[Insert your response transcript here, aim for 200-300 words\]*

*Please provide detailed feedback and suggestions for improvement based on the above criteria.*

### ***And make sure that you’re under time, with confidence and poise***

*The final thing to do is look at the details:*

* *Your timer*  
* *Your confidence and engagement*  
* *Your overall story telling and structure*

*These are things that are best done by looking at your video, or sending your video to someone.*

*You can also use the tool Poised for a subjective AI-based rating.*

---

## ***6\. Most Common Mistakes***

*Let’s end this with a quick recap of the mistakes to avoid.*

### ***Mistake 1 \- Include details that you can’t answer follow-up questions for***

*Being the first question in the interview, Tell Me About Yourself sets the stage for the rest. Any detail that piques people’s interest, they’re likely to ask a follow-up question about.*

*That’s why you should focus on details that you remember the context for:*

* *What was the situation?*  
* *What did you do specifically?*  
* *What were the counter metrics?*

*Knowing the intricacies of the features and examples you cite is key. You want the question to be a window into stories where you are the hero, not where others share the limelight.*

*And you definitely don’t want to blank on the details.*

### ***Mistake 2 \- Going too long***

*We’ve mentioned it a few times. It was even Principle 3\. But people consistently make this mistake.*

*Ideally, you should get into the habit of giving a 2-minute response. If you do enough practice with a timer in front of you, you can get there.*

*In my experience, just 3-4 hours of dedicated practice can get you from consistently going over to knowing exactly how to use 2 minutes for maximum impact.*

### ***Mistake 3 \- Not easy to follow narrative***

*If you recall Kartik’s coaching session, he actually had a round there where went from an 8 to a 7\. In an effort to cover off on all our strengths, it can be easy to lose a structure to your response.*

*You need to still build a compelling structure that the interviewer doesn’t need a whiteboard to track.*

*There should be a natural cadence \- even if it’s not the obvious chronological one. Even a simple, “here’s three experiences I want to highlight” works well.*

### ***Mistake 4 \- Not enough metrics***

*Ultimately, PMs these days are evaluated on their metrics:*

* *If you a PM for internal tools, it might simply be usage and CSAT. But you should nonetheless care about metrics.*  
* *If you are a growth PM, it should definitely include input and output financial metrics.*

*Be sure to cite these metrics in your question so they can see that you have a metrics focus, and are not just going to perpetuate a [feature factory](https://www.news.aakashg.com/p/pm-feature-factory).*

### ***Mistake 5 \- Not enough specific PM work and features***

*Especially amongst the aspiring PM set, there is this tendency to talk about work and impact that isn’t product work. That’s a mistake.*

*Even if you’re an experienced PM, you have to make sure to talk about PM work\!*

* *Customer discovery*  
* *Data analyzed*  
* *Cross-functional collaboration*

*People want to hear that you’re regularly shipping features that make an impact, and you drove the crucial insights that led to those features. Let’s expand on that list point…*

### ***Mistake 6 \- Not enough specifics of what you did to drive impact***

*I want to really drive this home as the last thing you hear. What did you, as a PM, do to drive the ultimate impact of the feature?*

* *Did you iterate on the design via user testing?*  
* *Did you write a bomber QA?*  
* *Was your [PRD](https://www.news.aakashg.com/p/product-requirements-documents-prds) next level?*  
* *Did you write a [FRW](https://www.news.aakashg.com/p/the-feature-results-writeup-an-advanced) before that lead to the direction?*

*Make your specific impact clear in the story, so that people can see that you are the type of PM who is driving insights that create impact.*

*If you do that for the areas they thought you were initially weak, you are golden.*
